q-95270.name: Question 1
q-95270.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

I. Any $3\times 4$ matrix $A$ has at most $4$ distinct singular values.

II. Any $8\times 6$ matrix $A$ has at most $8$ distinct singular values.

III. The matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]$ has one negative singular value.
q-95270.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Since $A$ is a $3\times 4$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $4\times 3$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $4\times 4$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{4\times 3}\times {A}_{3\times 4}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{4\times 4}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $4$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is false. Since $A$ is a $8\times 6$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $6\times 8$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $6\times 6$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{6\times 8}\times {A}_{8\times 6}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{6\times 6}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $6$ distinct singular values.

- Statement III is false.  All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, 
$A$  can't have a negative singular value.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

q-95279.name: Question 2
q-95279.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

I. The matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]$ has two negative singular values.

II. Any $4\times 5$ matrix $A$ has at most $5$ distinct singular values.

III. Any $8\times 4$ matrix $A$ has at most $8$ distinct singular values.
q-95279.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false.  All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, 
$A$  can't have any negative singular value.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, since $A$ is a $4\times 5$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $5\times 4$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $5\times 5$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{5\times 4}\times {A}_{4\times 5}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{5\times 5}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $5$ distinct singular values.

- Statement III is false. Since $A$ is a $8\times 4$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $4\times 8$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $4\times 4$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{4\times 8}\times {A}_{8\times 4}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{4\times 4}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $4$ distinct singular values.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

q-95377.name: Question 3
q-95377.problem: What are the singular values of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}]?$
q-95377.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -2 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ -2 & 8 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -2 & 0 \\ -2 & 8-\lambda  & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}8-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}|+2|\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )[(8-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-4)]+2(-2)(1-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-9\lambda +4)+(-4)(1-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-9\lambda +4-4) & =0 \\ \lambda (1-\lambda )(\lambda -9) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,1,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{1}=1 \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{0}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

What are the singular values of the matrix A=[0−2−11−20]?

a
4,2,0
b
3,1,0
c
9,1,0
d
1,1,0
e
9,3,1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The singular values of the matrix A are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ATA.

First, we calculate ATA:

ATA=[0−2−11−20]T[0−2−11−20]=[01−2−2−10][0−2−11−20]=[1−20−282021]

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ATA:

|ATA−λI|=0|1−λ−20−28−λ2021−λ|=0(1−λ)|8−λ221−λ|+2|−2201−λ|=0(1−λ)[(8−λ)(1−λ)−4)]+2(−2)(1−λ)=0(1−λ)(λ2−9λ+4)+(−4)(1−λ)=0(1−λ)(λ2−9λ+4−4)=0λ(1−λ)(λ−9)=0λ=9,1,0

Therefore, the singular values of A are as follows:

σ1=λ1=9=3σ2=λ2=1=1σ3=λ3=0=0

q-95378.name: Question 4
q-95378.problem: What are the singular values of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]?$
q-95378.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$  

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 1 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )((1-\lambda )^{2}-1) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(1-2\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}-1) & =0 \\ -\lambda (\lambda -1)(\lambda -2) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =2,\,1,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{2} \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{1}=1 \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{0}=0\end{aligned}
$$

q-139496.name: Question 5
q-139496.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

I. Any $5\times 3$ matrix $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.

II. Any $3\times 5$ matrix $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.

III. The singular values of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]$ are negative.
q-139496.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Since $A$ is a $5\times 3$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $3\times 5$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $3\times 3$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{3\times 5}\times {A}_{5\times 3}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{3\times 3}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is false. Since $A$ is a $3\times 5$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $5\times 3$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $5\times 5$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{5\times 3}\times {A}_{3\times 5}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{5\times 5}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $5$ distinct singular values.

- Statement III is false. All singular values of any matrix are non-negative.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

Question 5
?

Which of the following statements are true?

  1. Any 5×3 matrix A has at most 3 distinct singular values.
  2. Any 3×5 matrix A has at most 3 distinct singular values.
  3. The singular values of the matrix A=[−100−2] are negative.
a
I and II only
b
II only
c
I only
d
I and III only
e
II and III only
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The singular values of the matrix A are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ATA.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

  • Statement I is true. Since A is a 5×3 matrix and AT is a 3×5 matrix, ATA must be a 3×3 matrix: AT3×5×A5×3=ATA3×3 Hence, A has at most 3 distinct singular values.

  • Statement II is false. Since A is a 3×5 matrix and AT is a 5×3 matrix, ATA must be a 5×5 matrix: AT5×3×A3×5=ATA5×5 Hence, A has at most 5 distinct singular values.

  • Statement III is false. All singular values of any matrix are non-negative.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."
